sources.excerpt: DuckDuckGo has announced a successful no-logs audit of its VPN. It's not feature-rich, but it's a secure VPN and comes as part of the browsers privacy package
sources.text:
(Image credit: DuckDuckGo)
• Facebook

• Email
DuckDuckGo's VPN has passed an independent no-logs audit, with security firm Securitum confirming the service does not track user activity or store identifiable data.
The audit ran between October 2025 and January 2026 and included a full inspection of live servers, internal systems, and source code. Auditors checked how the VPN handles traffic, authentication, and infrastructure controls.
They found no evidence of logging mechanisms or data retention tied to individual users.
DuckDuckGo's product can't match the best VPNs, but it forms part of the company's privacy suite – and may be attractive to existing DuckDuckGo users.

No logging, no tracking – what the audit revealed
(Image credit: Pixabay)
An independent audit by Securitum found that DuckDuckGo does not log user activity on its VPN servers, validating its privacy policy and no-logs commitment.
Auditors conducted a technical review of live production systems, including source code inspection and infrastructure analysis, and found no mechanisms that track or store browsing data.
The report also confirmed that DuckDuckGo does not retain connection metadata such as DNS queries. The VPN uses an internal resolver with in-memory caching, which clears data after a set period and does not write logs to disk – limiting the ability to associate users with specific domains.
Securitum found that the VPN does not inspect user network traffic and operates without logging functions enabled. DuckDuckGo also separates authentication from VPN usage, issuing session tokens that are not linked to individual identities and clearing session data after each connection.
Additional findings showed that all VPN servers run a consistent no-logs configuration across regions and operate on dedicated infrastructure. Changes to logging-related systems require formal approval controls to reduce the risk of unintended data collection.
This audit follows a separate security audit completed in 2024 and supports DuckDuckGo's stated privacy policy, which maintains that the company has no way to tie VPN activity to individual users.

Basic protection, but a lack of advanced tools
DuckDuckGo VPN is included in the company's Privacy Pro subscription and runs through the DuckDuckGo browser – a privacy-focused alternative to Google Chrome.
It encrypts traffic across the entire device, hides a user's IP address from websites and services, and supports iOS, Android, Windows, and macOS, with up to 5 simultaneous connections.
The app offers a stripped-back interface with limited configuration and no deep server-level controls, which keeps setup quick but omits advanced features found in more established VPNs.
DuckDuckGo VPN does not rank among the top-tier VPN services. It lacks multi-hop routing, split tunneling, dedicated IP addresses, and streaming-optimized servers, all of which are common in VPNs like NordVPN or Surfshark.
Its $9.99 monthly price also more expensive than most long-term VPN plans. The best VPN deals see prices start at $1.11 per month, so considering exploring your options if the VPN is what attracts you to the DuckDuckGo subscription.
For the same price as DuckDuckGo Privacy Pro, you can subscribe to Proton Unlimited, and benefit from an entire privacy-focused ecosystem to rival Google.
That said, it can still make sense for existing DuckDuckGo users. The subscription adds a VPN alongside private search, tracker blocking, and email protection, giving users an extra layer of network-level privacy without managing a separate service. There's also private AI tools and identity theft protection.

sources.title: Proton VPN passes no-logs audit that found no user activity retention
sources.author: Alex Lekander
sources.excerpt: Proton VPN passed an independent audit of its no-logs policy, confirming that its infrastructure does not retain users' browsing activity.
sources.text:
Proton VPN passes no-logs audit that found no user activity retention
Proton VPN has passed the fifth consecutive independent audit of its no-logs policy, with European security firm Securitum concluding that the VPN provider’s infrastructure does not retain browsing activity, DNS queries, connection metadata, or records that could link users to specific VPN activity.
The latest assessment was conducted between May 20 and May 27, 2026, at Proton AG’s headquarters in Zürich, Switzerland. Two senior Securitum consultants spent six person-days reviewing Proton VPN’s production infrastructure to verify whether the service operates in accordance with its publicly stated no-logs commitments.
Proton is the Swiss company behind Proton Mail, Proton VPN, and other privacy-focused services. The company has made independent audits a core part of its transparency efforts, publishing both application security audits and annual reviews of its VPN infrastructure.
According to the audit report, Securitum examined selected production VPN servers from both Proton’s free and paid offerings, as well as VPN configuration files, deployment mechanisms, internal documentation, and operational procedures. The assessment was conducted on-site with Proton engineers demonstrating systems and configurations under the auditors’ direction.
The auditors found no evidence that Proton VPN’s infrastructure logs users’ browsing activity, DNS queries, destination websites, network traffic contents, or connection metadata that could be used to reconstruct a user’s online activity. Securitum also reported finding no persistent records that would allow Proton to associate a specific user with activity performed through a reviewed VPN server.
A key focus of the review was whether Proton could determine which websites or services a user accessed while connected to the VPN. Securitum concluded that the reviewed environment does not log or retain destination information in a user-attributable manner and does not maintain records showing which services were accessed through specific VPN servers. The auditors also found no persistent logging linking Proton accounts to particular VPN server connections.
Beyond verifying the absence of activity logs, Securitum examined the controls Proton has in place to prevent logging from being enabled without authorization. The auditors reviewed configuration management systems, monitoring tools, and alerting mechanisms designed to detect changes that could affect the VPN’s no-logs posture. They also verified the existence of a dual-approval workflow requiring privacy-related infrastructure changes to be reviewed and approved by another authorized employee before deployment.
The report further states that the same no-logs protections apply to both free and paid VPN servers, with auditors finding no differences that would result in less restrictive privacy protections for certain regions or subscription tiers. Active VPN configuration files reviewed during the assessment also contained no logging directives that would retain user-identifiable activity data.
As with previous assessments, Securitum noted that the audit represents a point-in-time review rather than a continuous guarantee. The engagement covered selected production server samples rather than Proton’s entire global VPN network, and conclusions were based on the systems, documentation, and evidence made available during the assessment period.
Despite those limitations, the auditors’ overall conclusion remained clear.
“The technical evidence reviewed during the engagement did not indicate that the examined Proton VPN server infrastructure logs users’ browsing activity, DNS queries, destination services, network traffic contents or user-identifiable connection metadata,” Securitum concluded. The firm added that it did not identify persistent records that would allow Proton to associate a specific user with activity performed through a reviewed VPN server.
The 2026 review marks the fifth consecutive annual no-logs audit conducted by Securitum since Proton began publishing independent assessments of its VPN infrastructure in 2022.

Best VPN for Streaming in 2026: Tested on 14 Services
© Gizmodo
Most people pay for more than one streaming service, and none of them works quite the same once you leave home. On a trip, shows vanish from your list, and live channels and whole apps show region errors instead of playing. Each service shows you a catalog based on where it thinks you are, so a VPN fixes it by connecting you through a server back home.
The hard part is finding one VPN that works on all of them, because every service has its own VPN detection. Out of the 40+ VPNs we’ve reviewed, these six unblocked the most services in our tests. The ranking comes first, then what each one unblocked.
Table of Contents

Best VPNs for Streaming in 2026
• NordVPN: Best VPN for streaming overall, with all 14 services unblocked
• Proton VPN: Best for private streaming, with Swiss privacy law and open-source apps
• ExpressVPN: Best for simple apps on every screen, from phones to Apple TV
• Surfshark: Best for unlimited devices on one subscription
• CyberGhost: Best for servers labeled by streaming service
• Private Internet Access: Best budget VPN for US services

Streaming Services Each VPN Unblocked
Every VPN faced the same 14 streaming services, with cookies and cache cleared before each session. Six services aren’t in the table. Channel 4, Peacock, and Now TV worked on all six VPNs, and PIA was the only one that couldn’t unblock HBO Max. Proton VPN couldn’t unblock Pluto TV, which also detected NordVPN now and then. The sixth worked in Surfshark’s app and through the browser extension on NordVPN and ExpressVPN.

Best VPN for Streaming: Detailed List
Every VPN in this ranking is a paid service. Free plans failed too often, and PrivadoVPN and Windscribe, the two that came closest, have their own section.

1. NordVPN: Best VPN for Streaming
Pros
• Hulu, ITVX, and JioHotstar unblocked
• Fast US servers
• No bandwidth caps
• Smart DNS for TVs and consoles
• Location spoofing in the Chrome extension
• Repeatedly audited no-log policy
Cons
• Occasional detection on Pluto TV and Prime Video
• Expensive monthly plans
NordVPN unblocked all 14 services we tried, a result only ExpressVPN matched. Pluto TV and Prime Video detected it now and then, and both played on the next attempt. One service detected the desktop app, and the Chrome extension unblocked it with location spoofing enabled, a setting that makes your browser report the VPN server’s location. Its US server tested at 181.50 Mbps on our 190.36 Mbps connection, the fastest US result we recorded.
The average speed loss across UK, US, and Japanese servers was 7.8%, which leaves far more speed than 4K requires. The network covers 152 countries. Smart DNS brings streaming to smart TVs and consoles without a VPN app: you enter a DNS address in the device’s network settings, and streaming services see the location you picked. NordVPN also has a native Apple TV app.
For households spread across several homes, Meshnet is one answer to Netflix’s password-sharing rules. Six independent audits since 2018 back its no-log policy. The Basic plan is under $3.50 a month on a two-year term.
Visit NordVPN

2. Proton VPN: Best Streaming VPN for Privacy
• Netflix US, Canada, and Japan unblocked
• BBC iPlayer and Channel 4 unblocked
• Swiss privacy law
• Open-source apps
• Stealth on every plan
• Native Apple TV app
• Doesn’t unblock Hulu or ITVX
• No Smart DNS
Proton VPN ranks second for viewers who want privacy alongside the big catalogs. It unblocked 10 of the 14 services, including Netflix in the US, Canada, and Japan on standard servers, BBC iPlayer, Prime Video, Peacock, and JioHotstar. It couldn’t unblock Hulu, Pluto TV, or ITVX, so if those are your main services, choose NordVPN instead.
Its average speed loss was 10.2%, and VPN Accelerator, which improves speed on long-distance connections, is enabled by default and made its US server 4.9% faster. Switzerland belongs to no intelligence-sharing pact, and Proton VPN publishes the source code of every app, so outside experts can check what it does. Securitum audits its no-log policy every year, and the network covers 149 countries.
Stealth disguises the connection as ordinary web traffic on networks that block VPNs, like school or office Wi-Fi. There’s an Apple TV app, but no Smart DNS for Samsung and LG TVs, so on those sets, you’d have to install Proton VPN on your router. On a two-year term, the VPN Plus plan costs under $3 a month and covers 10 devices.
Visit Proton VPN

3. ExpressVPN: Best for Simple Apps on Every Screen
• Hulu and JioHotstar unblocked
• Fast Japanese server
• WebRTC protection in the extension
• MediaStreamer for consoles
• High device limit
• Few advanced features
• High renewal price
ExpressVPN also unblocked all 14 services, with the same 7.8% average speed loss as NordVPN. Its Japanese server tested at 163.94 Mbps, the best Japan result we recorded, so Netflix Japan streamed as smoothly as Netflix US. ITVX and Prime Video detected it on some attempts, and like NordVPN, it required the browser extension for one service. The apps are simple to set up on every device, and the network covers 113 countries.
MediaStreamer, ExpressVPN’s Smart DNS, covers game consoles and smart TVs without VPN app support. That’s how a PlayStation connects through a VPN, and ExpressVPN also has a native tvOS app. The extensions add protection against WebRTC leaks, a browser feature that can reveal your IP address, but there’s no multi-hop and no malware filtering.
Its no-log policy is independently audited, and the Basic plan costs under $3 a month on a 28-month term. It renews at a much higher price, though, so note the renewal date when you subscribe. The ExpressVPN review has the rest.
Visit ExpressVPN

4. Surfshark: Best Streaming VPN for Unlimited Devices
• Fast UK server
• No device limit
• Camouflage Mode obfuscation
• CleanWeb ad filtering
• Doesn’t unblock ITVX
• Slow to connect at times
Surfshark unblocked 13 of the 14 services, including Hulu and JioHotstar, and it required no browser extension for any of them. ITVX was its only failure. Its UK server tested at 186.96 Mbps, the best UK result we recorded, and the average speed loss was 9.6%. One subscription covers every screen in a home, with no device limit, so the phones, tablets, laptops, and TVs of a whole family fit on one plan.
Camouflage Mode disguises VPN traffic on restrictive networks, CleanWeb strips ads from streaming sites, and Deloitte audited the no-log policy in 2023 and 2025. Its Android app unblocked the same services. Smart DNS is absent, so a Samsung or LG TV requires a router setup. Connections sometimes took a while to establish, so wait a few seconds before you try again.
On a 27-month term, the Starter plan costs about $2.50 a month, and Surfshark’s One plan adds antivirus for a little more.
Visit Surfshark

5. CyberGhost: Best for Servers Labeled by Streaming Service
• ITVX unblocked on its UK streaming server
• Smart DNS in several countries
• NoSpy servers it owns
• Quarterly transparency reports
• 24-hour desktop trial
• Doesn’t unblock Netflix Japan
• Low device limit
• No obfuscation
Picking a server takes no guesswork on CyberGhost, because the app labels servers by service: Netflix, BBC, Hulu, ITVX, and others. It unblocked 11 of the 14 services, including ITVX on its dedicated UK server, which Surfshark and Proton VPN couldn’t unblock. It couldn’t unblock Netflix Japan or JioHotstar, and the Japanese failure surprised me, since CyberGhost sells a server for that library.
Its average speed loss was 13.3%, with enough speed left for 4K. CyberGhost also has Smart DNS, and we explain how Smart DNS works here. CyberGhost owns its NoSpy servers, so no outside hosting company has access to them. It has published transparency reports every quarter since 2011 and covers 100 countries. The device limit is seven, which a big household can outgrow.
Nothing disguises the traffic on filtered networks, such as school or office Wi-Fi that blocks VPNs. CyberGhost also offers a 24-hour free VPN trial on Windows and macOS, an easy way to test it on your own services first.
Visit CyberGhost

6. Private Internet Access: Best Budget VPN for US Services
• Every US state covered
• Low starting price
• Court-tested no-log policy
• Dedicated IP add-on
• Doesn’t unblock Hulu or Prime Video on desktop
• Bigger speed loss in Japan
• Cluttered desktop interface
PIA does American content well and little else. Servers in all 50 states make it a strong choice for regional US services, and it unblocked Netflix US and Canada, Peacock, and BBC iPlayer. It couldn’t unblock Prime Video, Hulu, HBO Max, Netflix Japan, or JioHotstar, leaving 8 of the 14. Its average speed loss was 12.7%, and the Japanese server, at 141.61 Mbps, was it

For many people, a one-month VPN plan is all you need. Whether you're going on vacation or simply don't want to pay almost $100 upfront, paying monthly may be the way to go.
Of course, even the best VPNs want you to lock into a long-term contract, so paying monthly is usually the most expensive way of buying a VPN. Long-term plans offer massive discounts, and most also offer at least a 30-day money-back guarantee so you can try before you commit.
However, I've heard from many of my readers that flexibility is a primary concern. So, I've pulled together the very best cheap monthly VPN plans. Topping the list is Proton VPN, which is one of the best VPNs out there regardless of price. I've also included some other even cheaper options that aren't quite as polished, but still maintain good privacy.

The 3 best cheap monthly VPNs at a glance
Proton VPN | 1 month | $9.99Proton VPN is a highly regarded VPN provider that features in many of our guides. It focuses mainly on privacy, but has recently proven to be very effective for unblocking streaming sites, too. The monthly VPN plan is the best of the big names at $9.99, and prices drop to $2.99 per month on the 2-year plan. All subscriptions come with a 30-day money-back guarantee, including the 1-month plan.
Privado VPN | 1 month | $10.99Privado VPN is a simple and effective VPN, with great speeds and very effective streaming performance. Monthly subscriptions are affordable at $10.99, but longer plans are also incredibly cheap, starting at $20 all-in for 1 year. Be aware that 1-year plans have a 30-day money-back guarantee, but 1-month plans do not.
NordVPN | 1 month | $14.99From our testing, NordVPN is currently the best VPN overall. It's fast, secure, and very reliable for unblocking streaming sites. It's not the cheapest monthly VPN, but it's also not the most expensive at $14.99. Of course, longer plans offer better savings, starting at $3.49 per month for a 27-month subscription. There's a 30-day money-back guarantee on all subscriptions, including the 1-month plan.

How we chose the best monthly VPN plans
Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.
In our VPN reviews, alongside detailed price comparisons, we also focus on privacy, streaming performance, ease of use, and much more. Over the years, we've come across a lot of very cheap VPNs – and some pretty poor ones, too.
This guide's rankings have been determined by both quality and price. For example, Proton VPN is not the very cheapest monthly VPN, but it offers the best combination of top-tier VPN protection with a below-average monthly price. We have also featured cheaper providers like Mullvad, but further down the page due to their significant drawbacks.

Monthly price: $9.99 | Number of servers: 20,000+ | Server locations: 149 countries | Maximum devices supported: 10 | Customer support: Live chat, email, articles | Refund period: 30 days (any plan)

What we like:
Proton VPN is a top-quality VPN, and it ranks fourth in our overall guide to the best VPNs. If you just want a monthly plan, at $9.99 it's by far the best provider available for under $10. Considering some top VPNs like Surfshark charge over $15 for one month, this is great value.
In our testing, it was clear that Proton VPN as a whole is focused first and foremost on privacy. The apps are open-source, which means anyone can check the code for weaknesses, and in use we found them reliable and robust.
The Secure Core feature – special extra-secure servers – aren't cheap to maintain, but offer another level of privacy compared to rivals. Recent updates also include improvements to the Windows apps, and some welcome updates to the mobile apps' interfaces.
Proton VPN was also one of the very best VPNs for streaming in our latest round of VPN testing. It unblocked almost every streaming site we tried it with, including multiple Netflix locations, BBC iPlayer from outside the UK, and Disney Plus. Speeds are very impressive, too. In short, it covers all the bases.

What could improve:
There's not a lot to complain about with Proton VPN, but if you're a newbie, you might find the apps to be a little intimidating. They are by no means difficult to use, but if absolute simplicity is your priority, ExpressVPN or PrivadoVPN may suit you better.
A very specific gripe we have is that although Proton has updated the look of the apps on Windows, Android, and iOS, the Mac app has retained the old interface. It's not bad, but we'd like to see it updated soon to match the rest of the apps.
Finally, while not necessarily a negative, Proton VPN has removed the OpenVPN protocol from Android, Mac, and iOS apps. It's still available as a manual configuration, but it's not selectable in-app. This won't affect the vast majority of users, but those who need easy access to OpenVPN may want to look elsewhere.
🔒 Read our in-depth Proton VPN review for all the details.

Buy Proton VPN if:
✅ You prioritize privacy. Proton VPN is one of the most secure VPNs around, with plenty of privacy features as standard.
✅ You love streaming. Every streaming site we tried was unblocked by Proton VPN in our testing.
✅ You want the best bang for buck on a monthly plan. Proton VPN is the highest-quality VPN available at this price point.

Don't buy Proton VPN if:
❌ You want the simplest VPN possible. Proton isn't confusing, but absolute newbies may prefer something simpler.
❌ You need OpenVPN. This won't affect most people, but Proton's removal of OpenVPN means that if you need to use it, you'll need to manually configure it.

2. PrivadoVPN
PrivadoVPN is basic, but great value
Monthly price: $10.99 | Number of servers: 300+ | Server locations: 64 locations in 49 countries | Maximum devices supported: 10 | Customer support: Email, articles | Refund period: 30 days (monthly plan excluded)
What you see is what you get with PrivadoVPN. It's one of the cheapest VPNs around with no-nonsense apps, great connection speeds, and reliable unblocking for just about any site you can think of. The monthly plan is $10.99, and while that's a little more expensive than Proton VPN, it's still good value overall. If, after a month, you like PrivadoVPN, the 1-year plan costs $20, and the 2-year plan is just $30.
One of PrivadoVPN's standouts is that, despite having a much smaller fleet of servers than the big names, it manages very respectable speeds. When reviewing it, PrivadoVPN was almost as fast as NordVPN and Surfshark – two of the fastest VPNs. It's also just as good for streaming as the more established players.
Other than its price – which is hard to ignore – PrivadoVPN's biggest draw will be its simplicity. The interface is totally uncluttered – it's very similar to ExpressVPN's previous design – which means even those using a VPN for the first time will be able to get up and running in minutes.
Finally, Tom's Guide was able to visit PrivadoVPN's main data center in Amsterdam, and the whole setup was extremely secure and professional – always a good sign.
Our testing concluded that PrivadoVPN covered all the privacy basics well, but unlike many of the better-known providers, it has not undergone an independent audit of its privacy policy, apps, or server infrastructure. While not essential, these audits go a long way towards building a VPN's trustworthiness.
Unlike rivals like NordVPN and ExpressVPN, PrivadoVPN doesn't offer many added extras like a password manager or cyber insurance.The only extra is Control Tower, which is a smart DNS tool for blocking ads and malware. Admittedly, you may not need these – but they're certainly nice to have.
Finally, the single-month plan is non-refundable. Most other VPNs allow new customers to claim a refund on their first purchase, no matter the length of the plan. While PrivadoVPN does offer refunds on longer plans, it's not quite as generous to monthly subscribers.

sources.text:

• Proton VPN has passed its fifth annual independent no-logs audit
• The audit confirms the provider doesn't log any user-identifiable data
• Proton openly published the full report, criticizing competitors who don't
If you use a virtual private network to protect your digital life, you have to trust that the provider isn't secretly recording your every move. Thankfully, one of the top names in the industry has just proved its privacy claims are more than just marketing speak.
Following up on its fourth independent audit last year, Proton VPN has announced that it successfully passed a fifth consecutive annual third-party examination. Conducted by leading European security firm Securitum, the latest independent audit confirmed that the provider strictly adheres to its no-logs policy.
This means the company isn't tracking your IP address, logging the websites you visit, or storing your DNS queries. If you are looking for the best VPN to keep your online habits completely private, this independent verification that a provider is actually keeping its promises is exactly what you want to see.
According to Proton, its privacy claims have already been stress-tested in the real world. The provider notes that its no-logs policy has been tested in over 400 legal cases where it was ordered to turn over user data, but couldn't comply simply because the logs didn't exist.
Securitum is a heavy hitter in the cybersecurity space, overseeing more than 300 security testing projects every year for major corporations and banks. In addition to reviewing Proton VPN’s servers, the auditing firm recently completed a separate security audit of all Proton applications and found no significant vulnerabilities.

Looking under the hood
During this year's assessment, Securitum experts spent several days on-site examining VPN configuration files, assessing operating procedures, and interviewing staff to ensure that user data isn't being quietly collected.
The resulting 2026 report is clear. "The technical evidence reviewed during the engagement did not indicate that the examined Proton VPN server infrastructure logs users' browsing activity, DNS queries, destination services, network traffic contents, or user-identifiable connection metadata," the auditors concluded.
The assessment also found no persistent records that could tie a specific user to activity performed on a given server.
We are pleased to announce that Proton VPN has passed its 5th annual 3rd-party audit, confirming our strict no-logs policy.Unlike some providers, we openly publish full no-logs reports for anyone to read.Claims should be investigated & verified, including our own.1/2 👇June 16, 2026
Proton's dedication to peer review stems from its origins; the company was founded by scientists who met at CERN. Because of this, all Proton VPN apps are fully open source, meaning anyone with the technical know-how can inspect the code. The company also runs a bug bounty program to encourage security researchers to find and report potential flaws.
The provider also benefits from being headquartered in Switzerland. Under the current Swiss legal framework, Proton VPN is not subject to any mandatory data retention laws, which adds an extra layer of protection for users seeking a strictly private VPN.

Taking a swing at the competition
Alongside the positive audit results, Proton VPN took the opportunity to highlight its commitment to transparency, while throwing a little shade at rival providers.
In a blog post detailing the news, Proton CEO Andy Yen pointed out that the company publishes its full no-logs reports for anyone to read.
"Many of our competitors have never been independently audited or have performed a sleight-of-hand, getting their privacy policy audited instead of their actual no-logs infrastructure," wrote Yen.
Yen also criticized competitors who make their audits difficult to access, noting that some require users to sign non-disclosure agreements or only make the reports available to paying customers. While Proton made the full findings fully accessible here.

Mullvad VPN, NordVPN, and ExpressVPN were the fastest providers this quarter. They all have blended speed retention values of 55 percent or greater, unlike 60 percent of the VPNs tested this time around.

Which VPNs are fastest? | 2026-Q3 · tested Aug 2026
Editorial highlights from the full chart. Scores are a use-case-specific blend of 6 inputs — eu latency (p50), uk latency (p50), eu speed retention, uk speed retention, us speed retention, and bufferbloat (loaded latency) — weighted out of 10 (a use-case score, not each provider’s overall VPN rating).

What's in this article?

Mullvad VPN excels by keeping over 95% of the connection speed to UK servers, though users may experience some lag when the network is busy.
NordVPN keeps a solid portion of the connection speed across regions, but users might notice increased lag under load, particularly when the connection is busy.
ExpressVPN maintains a high percentage of the connection's speed in both EU and UK regions, although it struggles with lag when the connection is loaded.
Hotspot Shield leads by keeping up to 97% of the connection's speed, but suffers from significant lag when the connection is busy.
Surfshark keeps a consistent portion of the connection speed across regions, although it can experience noticeable lag during peak usage times.
Total VPN offers low latency but falls short in maintaining speed, particularly to US servers, and experiences moderate lag when busy.
CyberGhost keeps a substantial portion of the connection speed to UK servers, yet struggles in the EU and has moderate lag when the connection is busy.
Proton VPN keeps a decent portion of the connection speed to UK servers but has the highest latency to EU servers and noticeable lag when busy.
IPVanish offers minimal lag when the connection is busy, but its ability to keep speed, especially to US servers, leaves room for improvement.
PureVPN achieves the best latency results, particularly to UK servers, but maintains a lower percentage of the connection speed compared to competitors.
Lower-scoring providers from the full benchmark are left off this shortlist. Methodology · Full scorecard dataset

Why are some VPNs faster than others?
VPN performance depends on several factors including the protocol used, current server load, and each provider’s unique hardware configuration. Additionally, more-distant servers tend to be slower due to the increased time it takes data to travel there and back. If one VPN is significantly quicker than another, it may have better-optimized routing, higher-performance infrastructure, or less-congested servers.
Users can potentially improve their VPN’s performance by using a wired connection, choosing a closer server, and disabling obfuscation. Changing protocol may help but it’s not as simple as picking WireGuard over OpenVPN: protocol speeds are highly context-dependent. In other words, the fastest configuration for your device may not be the fastest for everyone.

What our data shows | 2026-Q3 · tested Aug 2026
Our top providers delivered high speed-retention rates, regardless of server location. That said, there was higher variance using US and EU servers (1.2 points and 1.1 points, respectively versus 0.6 points for British servers). This may be because the UK is a significantly smaller geographic region and as such, providers may be using the same or similar infrastructure as their competitors.

sources.excerpt: How much does a VPN cost? About $2 to $4 a month on a long plan, or $10 to $16 monthly. Compare 11 VPNs, renewals, and hidden costs.
sources.text:
How Much Does a VPN Cost in 2026?
© Gizmodo (VPN Cost Guide)
The price on a VPN’s homepage is rarely the price you pay per month. That headline figure usually assumes you pay for two years up front, and month-to-month billing for the same VPN can cost four or five times as much.
Then the first term ends, and the renewal arrives at a higher rate. So the honest answer depends on how long you commit, which plan tier you choose, and when you buy. Here’s what each of those choices does to the bill.
Table of Contents

VPN Prices at a Glance
• Long-term plans: about $2 to $4 a month for a well-known VPN, paid up front for two years or more.
• Month-to-month billing: about $10 to $16 a month for the same VPNs.
• Bundles with extra security tools: about $4 to $8 a month on a two-year plan.
• Renewal: usually two to three times the first-term monthly rate.
• Free plans: available from Proton VPN, Windscribe, and PrivadoVPN, with limits on servers, data, or devices.

VPN Prices Compared
The table lists approximate prices per month in US dollars, current as of November 2026. The long-plan price is the lowest monthly rate on a VPN’s longest plan, paid up front. Black Friday discounts are already live on several of them.

Across the nine VPNs in the table that sell both kinds of plan, month-to-month billing averages about $13. On the longest plan, the average falls to under $3 a month. Mullvad is the one exception to the pattern, since it charges a flat rate regardless of length. Astrill, meanwhile, is far more expensive than the rest.

The Best Value VPNs
For most people, these six offer the strongest value for what they cost:
• NordVPN: Best overall, at about $3.50 a month on its two-year Basic plan
• Proton VPN: Best for privacy, with a free plan if you’re not ready to pay
• ExpressVPN: Best for beginners, at about $3 a month on its Basic plan
• Private Internet Access: Best for the lowest renewal price, at around $2 a month
• Surfshark: Best for streaming value, with no device limit
• CyberGhost: Best for a longer refund window, at 45 days on long plans
NordVPN is the #1-rated VPN in our rankings, yet its price is near the middle of the table. The best VPN options rarely cost the most, as long as you buy a long plan.
Get NordVPN

Why Do VPNs Cost So Much?
A VPN company pays for servers in dozens of countries, the bandwidth they use, staff to keep apps updated, and independent audits of its privacy claims. Four choices on your side then decide how much of that cost ends up on your bill.

Subscription Length
Start with the plan length, because VPNs charge less per month the longer you commit. Take NordVPN, the best option overall. Month-to-month, it costs about $15, so two years of monthly billing would cost about $360.
Its two-year plan, by contrast, adds three free months, and its Basic plan costs about $3.50 a month. That’s under $100 for 27 months, paid at checkout. No NordVPN coupon is required for that rate, either.
Every VPN in the table works the same way, apart from Mullvad. Long plans keep subscribers for longer, so VPN companies reward the commitment with a lower rate.

Plan Tier and Extra Features
The second choice is the tier. NordVPN’s Basic plan is the VPN alone, while Complete adds next-gen antivirus against malware and phishing, plus a password manager and 1 TB of encrypted cloud storage. Prime adds identity theft protection for US subscribers.
Surfshark and NordVPN follow the same ladder: Surfshark’s One plan adds antivirus to the Starter plan. Each step up usually costs another $1 to $4 a month on a long plan. If you already pay for a password manager or antivirus, the Basic or Starter plan is enough.
During sales, however, the gap can shrink to nothing: this season, Surfshark sells its One plan for the Starter price.

Server Network Size
Large networks are expensive to operate, since every server requires hosting, bandwidth, and maintenance. Even so, a big network doesn’t have to mean a high price. Private Internet Access covers more than 100 countries with servers in every US state, and it’s one of the cheapest VPNs in the table.
Network size is a clearer dividing line between free and paid VPNs. Free plans usually offer a handful of countries, while paid ones cover around 100 or more. A dedicated IP address, a fixed IP address that only you use, costs extra on most VPNs.

Streaming and Torrenting
Streaming services block VPN servers they detect, so keeping Netflix or BBC iPlayer working is an ongoing cost for the VPN company.
Free plans often don’t unblock streaming services, and some block torrenting. Streaming and torrenting are the most popular reasons to use a VPN, so this is often what you pay for.

Hidden Costs: Renewals, Taxes, and Add-Ons
The checkout price is only the first part of the bill. These are the costs that show up later:
• Renewal price: once the first term ends, most VPNs renew at two to three times the introductory monthly rate. Private Internet Access and CyberGhost increase the least, and NordVPN increases the most.
• Automatic renewal: plans renew unless you disable auto-renewal in your account, and the renewal is often a one-year term.
• Sales tax: NordVPN, ExpressVPN, and Surfshark add tax at checkout where it applies, so the final charge can exceed the advertised rate.
• Add-ons: a dedicated IP address usually costs a few dollars a month on top of the plan, and some VPNs sell antivirus separately.
• Refund rules on short plans: CyberGhost’s monthly plan has a 14-day refund window, compared with 45 days on its longer plans.
A two-year plan still costs less in total than paying monthly, even after renewal. Still, compare the renewal price before you buy, because it decides what the third year costs you.

Expensive vs Cheap VPNs: Should You Always Pay More?
In most shops, a higher price buys better quality. With VPNs, a paid VPN is better than a free one, but a more expensive paid VPN isn’t automatically better than a cheaper one. Take NordVPN and Astrill VPN, which costs $30 a month.
NordVPN costs about a ninth as much on its long plan and offers more for the money: Double VPN, next-gen antivirus on the Complete plan, unlimited data, and servers in more countries. Astrill’s main advantage is that it’s better known for working in China. Even on its two-year plan, Astrill costs about $12.50 a month.
NordVPN’s top Prime plan, with identity theft protection added, costs less than that on its own two-year term. So don’t treat a high price as proof of quality. The opposite warning applies too. A VPN that’s suspiciously cheap, or free with no paid plan, often makes its money from your data.
The paid VPNs in the table have independently audited no-logs policies or a long privacy record, and that’s part of what you pay for.
Check Out NordVPN

How Much Does a Business VPN Cost?
Business VPNs charge per user, and they cost more because they add a central admin panel, user management, and dedicated servers for the company. NordLayer, from the team behind NordVPN, starts at about $8 per user a month on annual billing, with a 5-user minimum.
Proton VPN for Business starts at about $7 per user a month. Plans that include a dedicated server, so staff can reach company systems from a fixed IP address, add roughly $40 a month per server.
For a sole trader or a small team without shared systems, a consumer plan from NordVPN or Proton VPN covers the same basic protection for less.

How to Cut the Total VPN Cost
A VPN is one of the easier subscriptions to pay less for, because the discounts are large and predictable. These tips make the biggest difference.

Choose a Long-Term Plan
Long-term plans offer the biggest discount. Choose a one-year or two-year plan, pay for the whole term at once, and the monthly cost drops from over $10 to $2 or $3. If you plan to use a VPN for privacy every day, this is the cheapest way to do it.

Don’t Always Choose the Longest Plan
That said, a long plan only pays off if you keep using it. Some people use a VPN for a week or two: a trip to a country that blocks websites, or a holiday when you want to watch TV from home. For them, one month at $10 to $15 costs far less than two years paid at once.
Timing helps as well. Most VPNs offer their deepest discounts in late November, and the current Black Friday VPN deals are already live.
If the lowest monthly rate is the priority, the cheapest VPNs that are still safe are compared side by side, with their renewal prices.

Use a Free Trial, Free Plan, or Refund Window
You don’t always have to pay to test a VPN. NordVPN and ExpressVPN offer short free trials on Android, and Pri

sources.excerpt: Independent auditors found no evidence of logging for the third time
sources.text:
(Image credit: IPVanish)

• Schellman Compliance’s latest audit of IPVanish has confirmed no traffic, metadata, or session logging
• The audit is the third since 2022, and marks the second audit since IPVanish committed to annual audits
• It follows IPVanish’s recent RAM-only server rollout and expansion to a 150-location network
IPVanish has announced the results of its third independent no-logs audit, and once again its privacy claims have a clean bill of health.
The audit was completed by Schellman Compliance, a leading provider of attestation services, on September 25, 2026.
Following two previous third-party audits in 2022 and 2025, the review is the latest in what's become an annual tradition for the VPN provider: inviting an outside firm to poke holes in its no-logs policy.
According to the results shared, the policy is accurate and fully aligned with IPVanish’s public privacy commitments – with its zero-logs promise strictly enforced across the company’s global server network.

Proof, not promises
The evaluation was comprehensive. Schellman’s auditors were given unrestricted access to IPVanish’s systems, configurations, and teams.
Interviews were conducted with engineering and operations staff, and company workflows were reviewed alongside infrastructure, internal documentation, and the administrative procedures governing the VPN app itself.
They also ran test traffic exercises – simulating real-world scenarios and watching closely for any evidence of VPN logging, including DNS queries, VPN metadata, and server responses.
The conclusion: no records of browsing traffic, session history, or connection metadata are collected or stored on active servers. Further, any real-time systems used to detect network abuse operate purely in memory, leaving nothing behind.
The auditors also checked IPVanish’s internal safeguards, confirming that any changes to how its servers work need sign-off from multiple people. This makes it much harder for logging to be quietly switched back on.
“A no-logs policy is only as credible as the evidence behind it,” said Subbu Sthanu, General Manager, Consumer Cybersecurity at IPVanish.
“People shouldn’t have to rely on promises when it comes to their privacy. By committing to annual independent audits of our no-logs policy, we’re making transparency and accountability an ongoing practice, not a one-time exercise.”
Customers who want to dig deeper can download the full report themselves via the Security Reports page in the My IPVanish account portal.

Part of a bigger picture
The audit doesn’t arrive in isolation. IPVanish has spent the past year restructuring its plans – Essential, Complete, and Advanced – around a suite of security extras, while growing a server network that now spans more than 150 locations.
Meanwhile, the company is midway through migrating its infrastructure to RAM-only servers, which wipe all data on every reboot and eliminate the possibility of storage-based logging; it has pledged to complete that transition by 2027.
Taken together, the picture is of a provider treating privacy less as a marketing slogan and more as something baked into how it operates.
In a market where rivals like NordVPN and ExpressVPN have made repeat audits their own baseline, the third-party stamp of approval is now a must-have rather than a nice-to-have. IPVanish seems intent on keeping up.
Mark is a Tech Security Writer for TechRadar and has been published on Comparitech and IGN. He graduated with a degree in English and Journalism from the University of Lincoln and spent several years teaching English as a foreign language in Spain. The Facebook-Cambridge Analytica data scandal sparked Mark’s interest in online privacy, leading him to write hundreds of articles on VPNs, antivirus software, password managers, and other cybersecurity topics. He recently completed the Google Cybersecurity Certificate, and when he's not studying for the CompTIA Security+ exam, Mark can be found agonizing over his fantasy football team selections, watching the Detroit Lions, and battling bugs and bots in Helldivers 2.
